description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary jewel from Oaxaca, Mexico, renowned for its incredible depth of flavor and dark, velvety texture. This iconic sauce is a complex symphony of dried chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and a touch of chocolate, creating a truly unforgettable dining experience. It's traditionally served with poultry, making it a centerpiece for special occasions and family gatherings.

instructions.title: Prepare Chiles
instructions.text: Lightly toast the dried chiles in a dry skillet over medium heat for 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Be careful not to burn them. Transfer the toasted chiles to a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 15 minutes. Drain and set aside.

instructions.title: Sauté Aromatics and Spices
instructions.text: In a large skillet, heat 1 tablespoon of lard or oil. Add the sliced plantain, tomatoes, tomatillos, onion, and garlic. Cook until softened and lightly browned, about 5-7 minutes. Add the almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, raisins, tortilla pieces, cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, and anise seeds. Cook for another 3 minutes, stirring constantly.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Base
instructions.text: Transfer the rehydrated chiles, sautéed aromatics, nuts, seeds, and spices to a blender. Add 2 cups of chicken broth. Blend until a very smooth paste forms. This may take a few minutes. Add more broth if needed to aid blending.

instructions.title: Strain the Mole
instructions.text: Set a fine-mesh sieve over a large pot or Dutch oven. Pour the blended mole mixture through the sieve, pressing firmly with a spatula to extract all the liquid and pulp. Discard any remaining solids in the sieve. This step is crucial for a smooth, velvety mole.

instructions.title: Simmer and Thicken
instructions.text: Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon of lard or oil in the same pot over medium heat. Add the strained mole mixture and bring it to a gentle simmer. Stir in the Mexican chocolate until it has fully melted and incorporated. Continue to simmer, stirring frequently, for at least 15-20 minutes, or until the mole has thickened to your desired consistency. Add remaining chicken broth as needed to reach desired consistency. Season with salt to taste.

instructions.title: Serve Mole Negro
instructions.text: Your Oaxacan Black Mole is ready! Serve it warm over cooked chicken, turkey, or pork. It is traditionally accompanied by white rice and warm corn tortillas. Garnish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds if desired.

tips: For a truly authentic flavor, ensure your chiles are properly toasted but not burnt before rehydrating. This brings out their smoky notes.
If you cant find all chile varieties, you can substitute with a mix of dried Ancho and Mulato chiles for a similar dark color and flavor profile.
Mole Negro tastes even better the next day as the flavors deepen. Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.
article:
The aroma alone is enough to transport you. A deep, complex symphony of earthy chilies, toasted nuts, warm spices, and a hint of dark chocolate – this is the magic of Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro), a dish revered as the "King of Moles" in Mexico. Far more than just a sauce, Mole Negro is a culinary masterpiece, a testament to generations of Oaxacan culinary tradition, and a perfect centerpiece for any Mexican dinner recipes repertoire.

Originating from the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca, known as "the land of seven moles," Mole Negro stands out for its incredibly rich, dark color and unparalleled depth of flavor. It's a dish of celebration, often served at weddings, fiestas, and special family gatherings, embodying the very soul of Mexican gastronomy. While its list of ingredients might seem daunting, the process is a labor of love that yields a reward far greater than the sum of its parts – a truly unforgettable dining experience.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)?

Oaxacan Black Mole, or Mole Negro, is arguably the most intricate and celebrated of all Mexican moles. Its signature deep, almost black hue comes from a careful roasting process of several types of dried chilies, including chilhuacle negro, mulato, ancho, and pasilla Oaxaca, along with other dark ingredients. Unlike simpler moles, Mole Negro boasts a flavor profile that is simultaneously sweet, savory, smoky, spicy, and subtly bitter, creating an incredibly balanced and harmonious taste.

The complexity of Mole Negro stems from the sheer number of ingredients – often 20 to 30, and sometimes even more – each meticulously prepared. Key components include a variety of dried chilies, toasted nuts and seeds (almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds), warm spices (cloves, cinnamon, black pepper, cumin), aromatics (onion, garlic), fruits (plantain, raisins), vegetables (tomatoes, tomatillos), a thickener (stale tortillas or bread), and crucially, Mexican chocolate. The laborious process of toasting, rehydrating, grinding, and slow-cooking these ingredients is what develops the legendary depth that makes Oaxacan Black Mole so unique and cherished. It's a dish that tells a story with every spoonful, a true cultural emblem of Oaxaca.

## Ingredients You Need for Oaxacan Black Mole

Making authentic Oaxacan Black Mole at home is a rewarding challenge. While some ingredients might require a trip to a specialty Mexican grocery store, the effort is well worth it. Here's a comprehensive list of what you'll need:

**For the Chilies:**
* 4-5 Mulato chilies
* 4-5 Ancho chilies
* 3-4 Pasilla Oaxaca chilies (or Pasilla Negro if Oaxaca variety is unavailable)
* 2-3 Chipotle chilies (for a smoky kick, optional)
* 1-2 Chilhuacle Negro chilies (highly recommended if you can find them, for true authenticity)
* 6-8 cups chicken or vegetable broth, plus more for soaking

**For the Aromatics & Vegetables:**
* 1 large white onion, roughly chopped
* 6-8 cloves garlic, peeled
* 2 ripe roma tomatoes, roughly chopped
* 2 small tomatillos, husked and quartered
* 1 ripe plantain, peeled and sliced
* 1-2 stale corn tortillas, torn
* 1 slice of stale bread (bolillo or baguette), torn

**For the Nuts & Seeds:**
* 1/4 cup raw almonds
* 1/4 cup raw peanuts
* 2 tablespoons sesame seeds, plus more for garnish
* 1 tablespoon pumpkin seeds (pepitas)

**For the Spices:**
* 1 teaspoon whole black peppercorns
* 1/2 teaspoon whole cloves
* 1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds
* 1 small stick true cinnamon (Canela), about 1 inch
* 1/4 teaspoon star anise (optional)

**For the Sweetness & Fat:**
* 1/4 cup raisins or prunes
* 1-2 ounces Mexican chocolate (tabletas), dark variety
* 1 small piece piloncillo (Mexican brown sugar cone), or 1-2 tablespoons dark brown sugar
* 1/4 cup lard or vegetable oil, plus more for frying

**Other:**
* Salt to taste

## Step-by-Step Instructions to Make Mole Negro

Patience is your most important ingredient when making Mole Negro. This process is involved but incredibly fulfilling.

1.  **Prepare the Chilies:** Carefully remove stems and most of the seeds from all dried chilies. Heat a comal or dry skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the chilies in batches for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant and slightly puffed, being careful not to burn them (which would make them bitter). Place toasted chilies in a large heatproof bowl, cover with hot broth, and let them rehydrate for 20-30 minutes until soft.

2.  **Toast Nuts and Seeds:** In the same dry skillet, toast the almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, and pumpkin seeds separately until lightly golden and fragrant. Set aside.

3.  **Sauté Aromatics and Other Ingredients:** Heat 1-2 tablespoons of lard or oil in a large skillet or Dutch oven. Sauté the chopped onion and garlic until softened. Add the tomatoes, tomatillos, plantain, raisins/prunes, stale tortillas, and bread. Cook until the vegetables are softened and the plantain is slightly caramelized. Remove from heat.

4.  **Grind Spices:** In a spice grinder or molcajete, grind the black peppercorns, cloves, cumin seeds, and cinnamon stick until finely powdered.

5.  **Combine and Blend:** Drain the rehydrated chilies, reserving the soaking liquid. In a high-speed blender, combine the rehydrated chilies, sautéed aromatics and vegetables, toasted nuts and seeds, and ground spices. Add about 1-2 cups of the reserved chili soaking liquid (or fresh broth) to help blend. Blend until the mixture is as smooth as possible. This may take several minutes and require adding more liquid gradually.

6.  **Strain for Smoothness (Optional but Recommended):** For a truly authentic, silky smooth Oaxacan Black Mole, pass the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve or colander, pressing hard with a spatula to extract all the liquid and flavor, leaving behind only the fibrous solids. Discard the solids. This step is time-consuming but yields a superior texture.

7.  **Cook the Mole:** Heat 1/4 cup of lard or vegetable oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Carefully pour the strained mole paste into the hot oil. **Be cautious, as it will splatter.** Stir constantly for 15-20 minutes. This "frying" step is crucial for developing the mole's deep flavor and darkening its color.

8.  **Simmer and Season:** Gradually add the remaining broth, stirring continuously to prevent sticking. Add the Mexican chocolate and piloncillo (or brown sugar). Bring the mole to a gentle simmer, then reduce heat to low. Cook, stirring frequently, for at least 1-2 hours, or up to 3-4 hours, allowing the flavors to meld and the mole to thicken to a rich, velvety consistency. If it becomes too thick, add more broth or water.

9.  **Adjust Seasoning:** Taste and adjust salt, sugar, and acidity as needed. The balance should be complex – a little sweet, a little savory, a little spicy, and a little bitter.

## Pro Tips for the Best Oaxacan Black Mole

*   **Patience is Paramount:** Mole Negro is a labor of love. Don't rush any step, especially the toasting of chilies and nuts, and the final simmering.
*   **Quality Ingredients:** Seek out fresh, high-quality dried chilies. If you can find Chilhuacle Negro chilies, they are essential for the authentic Oaxacan Black Mole flavor.
*   **Don't Burn the Chilies:** When toasting chilies, a brief toast is all you need. Burnt chilies will make your mole bitter.
*   **The Power of Straining:** While optional, straining the blended paste through a fine-mesh sieve is the secret to a professional-grade, silky smooth mole. It removes any remaining chili skins or fibrous bits.
*   **Fry the Paste Thoroughly:** The initial frying of the mole paste in oil is critical. It deepens the flavor, darkens the color, and helps prevent it from tasting raw.
*   **Slow Simmer for Depth:** The longer your mole simmers on low heat, the more the flavors will meld and deepen. It truly tastes better the next day.
*   **Balance the Flavors:** Taste frequently and adjust. If it's too bitter, add a touch more piloncillo or chocolate. If it's bland, a pinch more salt or a squeeze of lime can help.

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

Oaxacan Black Mole is most famously paired with poultry, creating classic Mexican dinner recipes.

*   **Mole Negro con Pollo (Chicken in Black Mole):** This is the quintessential serving. Simmer cooked chicken pieces (thighs, drumsticks, or breast) directly in the finished mole sauce until heated through and coated.
*   **Pavo en Mole (Turkey in Mole):** For special occasions, like Thanksgiving, turkey is a traditional pairing.
*   **Enchiladas de Mole:** Fill corn tortillas with shredded chicken, roll them, cover generously with warm Oaxacan Black Mole, and bake until bubbly. Garnish with crumbled queso fresco, thinly sliced red onion, and sesame seeds.
*   **Vegetarian Options:** Serve over roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or hearty black bean cakes. It's also fantastic with tamales.
*   **Sides:** Always serve with warm corn tortillas (for scooping up every last drop!), fluffy Mexican rice, and refried beans.
*   **Garnish:** A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds and a sprig of fresh cilantro are simple yet elegant garnishes. A dollop of Mexican crema can add a touch of richness.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the classic Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is sacred to many, home cooks can make minor adjustments based on availability and preference.

*   **Chili Variations:** If you can't find chilhuacle negro, you can increase the amount of mulato and ancho chilies, and perhaps add a bit more chipotle for smokiness. Experiment with other dark dried chilies like chilhuacle rojo for nuanced flavor.
*   **Nuts and Seeds:** While almonds, peanuts, and sesame are traditional, you can adjust the ratios or even include a few pecans or walnuts for a different nutty undertone.
*   **Sweeteners:** Piloncillo is best, but dark brown sugar is a suitable substitute. Adjust to your desired sweetness level.
*   **Chocolate:** Authentic Mexican chocolate is key, but if unavailable, use a high-quality dark unsweetened chocolate (70% cacao or higher) and adjust the piloncillo/sugar accordingly.
*   **Thickeners:** Besides tortillas and bread, some recipes use corn masa or even a few masa harina tortillas to thicken.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan Mole:** For a plant-based version, use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth and vegetable oil instead of lard. The rest of the ingredients are naturally plant-based. Serve with plant-based protein or vegetables.

Embarking on the journey to make Oaxacan Black Mole is an culinary adventure that promises rich rewards. It’s a dish that transcends mere sustenance, offering a taste of history, culture, and the profound culinary artistry of Oaxaca. Whether for a special occasion or simply to elevate your weeknight Mexican dinner recipes, this Mole Negro will leave an indelible mark on your palate and your cooking repertoire.
